item.text: I’ll read the five map parts in order, place each new note, write the JSONL update, and run the requested check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<20:130 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
20:130/q01 What speech must the Prophet endure, and why? [فَٱصْبِرْ عَلَىٰ مَا يَقُولُونَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the command is read primarily against the opponents' speech and its delayed punishment or as inward formation under divine decree.)
  20:130/q01/p1 He must endure hostile denials, insults, and demands for punishment until God's appointed judgment, while continuing his mission. — reasons: Muqatil specifies denial of threatened punishment; Yahya, Tabari, Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Razi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur list accusations including sorcery, madness, poetry, lying and soothsaying. Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur relate patience to the fixed time of punishment; Razi adds continued preaching, and Islahi relates it to pressure from those demanding punishment.
  20:130/q01/p2 He should patiently accept God's decree, recognizing that opponents act under divine power and that their objections train him spiritually. — reasons: Qashani presents patience through God and divine decree; Bursevi transmits the Najmi inward interpretation. Tabatabai joins acceptance of delayed judgment to rejecting shirk and praising God.
20:130/q02 What does patience mean here as a virtue? [فَٱصْبِرْ · interpretation]
  20:130/q02/p1 It is self-restraint appropriate to reason and divine law, expressed differently in battle, calamity, and silence; enduring abuse can be good or obligatory. — reasons: Bursevi quotes Raghib's definition and his examples of courage, broadness of chest and keeping silent, with 2:177, 22:35 and 33:35; Jishumi says endurance of abuse is praiseworthy and sometimes obligatory.
20:130/q03 Was the command to endure their speech abrogated by fighting? [فَٱصْبِرْ عَلَىٰ مَا يَقُولُونَ · sciences] (turns on: Whether patient endurance of speech is incompatible with the later command to fight.)
  20:130/q03/p1 Yes; the later fighting command ended the earlier permission or duty simply to endure abuse. — reasons: Wahidi says God subsequently decreed their killing; Ibn Jawzi and the reported Kalbi-Muqatil, Baghawi and Bursevi accounts cite the fighting or sword verse.
  20:130/q03/p2 No; combat and patience under verbal abuse can coexist, so the command remains applicable. — reasons: Jishumi argues that the passages do not conflict; Qurtubi reports that fighting did not eradicate all unbelievers; al-Kabir says fighting need not end endurance of speech; Alusi reads patience as composure, not cessation of fighting.
20:130/q04 What does the command to glorify God require here? [وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether tasbih names ritual prayer, direct remembrance and transcendence, or an inward spiritual process; the time phrases and context are used to decide.)
  20:130/q04/p1 It means prayer, including praise and glorification, at the specified times. — reasons: Tabari explains prayer while praising God; Bursevi calls tasbih a part naming the whole; Ibn Ashur says prayer includes glorification. Most commentators in Razi and the early authorities map the phrases to prayers. Razi prefers the complete five-prayer construal among prayer interpretations; Tabatabai notes that this is the majority's identification, though the word alone does not compel it. Muqatil links the command to hoped-for afterlife reward.
  20:130/q04/p2 It means declaring God's transcendence and majesty through remembrance, in speech, thought or action, rather than specifying ritual prayer. — reasons: Abu Muslim and Razi relate this reading to countering the opponents' denial and shirk; Razi considers it closer to context. Ibn Atiyya allows the formula subhan Allah wa bihamdihi after dawn and before sunset and cites seventy glorifications; Tabarsi allows continuous praise; Abu Hayyan distinguishes a spoken formula from semantic exaltation; al-Izz calls the ba instrumental and says negating deficiency affirms perfection. Alusi notes both an objection from specified times and a reply taking them as signs of continuity; Tabatabai says the night part complicates that reply. Kur'an Yolu cites the prayer chronology.
  20:130/q04/p3 It signifies inward stripping of selfhood and manifestation of the Lord's qualities, with spiritual illumination across the named times. — reasons: Qashani reads the rising and setting as disclosure and concealment of spirit and night as the veiled ego; the Study Quran transmits Aj's path of patience and remembrance until selfhood vanishes and the Beloved is witnessed.
20:130/q05 How does prayer or remembrance help the Prophet endure? [فَٱصْبِرْ وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ · interpretation]
  20:130/q05/p1 It brings solace, perseverance and divine aid amid abuse and hardship. — reasons: Razi compares 2:45 and says remembrance gives rest; Biqai says worship raises the soul; Bursevi cites 13:28 and the Prophet's recourse to prayer in distress; Alusi compares 2:45 and 2:153. Islahi extends the lesson to community hardship and says prayer teaches that events follow God's will for good, while the Prophet's role is to teach as well as recite. Ibn Ashur directs attention from worldly comforts to spiritual purification and the God-fearing outcome.
20:130/q06 How is bi-ḥamdi rabbika construed? [بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ · grammar] (turns on: The force of ba and whether praise is annexed to its agent or object.)
  20:130/q06/p1 It is circumstantial accompaniment: glorify or pray while praising God, especially for His help, guidance and blessings. — reasons: Tabari makes the praise God's object by comparison with an Arabic verbal noun construction; Kashshaf, Razi and Nasafi specify praise for enabling prayer; Baydawi adds guidance and blessings. Alusi takes the ba as accompaniment and praise as an object-directed verbal noun; Ibn Ashur calls it a circumstantial phrase with an agent relation; Samin likewise calls it a hal.
  20:130/q06/p2 The ba is instrumental, and divine praise may be understood as God's own praise of Himself. — reasons: Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam permits agent, object and specifying annexation; Alusi prefers agent annexation because perfectly true praise is God's praise of Himself.
20:130/q07 Which worship is indicated before sunrise? [قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ ٱلشَّمْسِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the temporal instruction specifies obligatory Fajr or includes direct and optional morning remembrance.)
  20:130/q07/p1 The dawn or Fajr prayer. — reasons: This is the repeated mapping from Muqatil onward. Ibn Ashur says the prayer times are clarified by mass-transmitted Sunna; the Jarir and two-asr reports identify the morning prayer; Biqai includes it at the first endpoint.
  20:130/q07/p2 The time also accommodates direct glorification and remembrance after dawn, extending toward the forenoon prayer. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites the formula through the two Duha rakas; Abu Hayyan reports it. Bursevi transmits a report valuing remembrance until sunrise above freeing eighty descendants of Ishmael. Islahi includes ishraq.
20:130/q08 Which worship is indicated before sunset? [وَقَبْلَ غُرُوبِهَا · interpretation] (turns on: How broadly before sunset is taken, and whether tasbih is prayer or direct remembrance.)
  20:130/q08/p1 The afternoon or Asr prayer. — reasons: A widespread mapping supported by the Jarir report, the two-asr report transmitted by Durr and Alusi, and ordinary pre-sunset usage as Alusi observes. Alusi's note calling the sunset prayer here differs from his later alternative.
  20:130/q08/p2 Both noon or Dhuhr and afternoon or Asr prayers. — reasons: They both fall after solar noon and before sunset, according to Bursevi and Alusi; Nasafi calls both part of the latter half of day. Razi reports Ibn Abbas's complete five-prayer mapping; Ibn Ashur allows this alongside Asr alone.
  20:130/q08/p3 The sunset prayer. — reasons: Alusi calls the pre-sunset phrase the sunset prayer in one note, while elsewhere he reports the Asr and Dhuhr-Asr readings.
  20:130/q08/p4 Direct glorification before sunset, including a repeated formula. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports seventy glorifications before sunset bring forgiveness; Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit the sunset report.
20:130/q09 What do ānāʾ al-layl mean lexically? [ءَانَآئِ ٱلَّيْلِ · meaning]
  20:130/q09/p1 The hours, periods or watches of night; several singular forms are transmitted. — reasons: Majaz cites the Hudhali poet al-Mutanakhkhal or Abu Athila; Tabari cites a line attributed to al-Munkhil al-Sadi; Wahidi cites al-Asha; Jishumi and Ibn Atiyya cite a Hudhali line. Qurtubi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur list variant singulars including ini, inu, ina and ana; Tabatabai derives the plural from ina or inw; Alusi cites Raghib's parallel at 33:53 and al-Hutay'a on delaying supper.
20:130/q10 Which night worship do the night hours designate? [وَمِنْ ءَانَآئِ ٱلَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the phrase specifies one or two fixed evening prayers, spans all or part of night, or adds voluntary worship.)
  20:130/q10/p1 The sunset and nightfall prayers, Maghrib and Isha. — reasons: Qatada and Ibn Abbas transmissions place both in early night; Baydawi and Bursevi add that quiet and inclination to rest make this worship demanding. Alusi sees the renewed command and fronted hours as emphasis.
  20:130/q10/p2 The Isha prayer specifically. — reasons: Tabari first glosses the evening prayer after a portion of night and reports Ibn Zayd; Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, Nasafi and Study Quran give Isha alone; Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan use nightfall prayer.
  20:130/q10/p3 Prayer or remembrance throughout the whole night. — reasons: Ibn Abbas is reported by Tabari, Mawardi and Tabrisi; al-Hasan spells out beginning, middle and end in Tabari and Ibn Jawzi.
  20:130/q10/p4 The middle of the night. — reasons: Ibn Abbas is reported with this more restricted time by Tabari and Ibn Jawzi.
  20:130/q10/p5 The beginning of the night. — reasons: Baghawi transmits Ibn Abbas's early-night interpretation; Tabri
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<20:130 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
si relates it to Maghrib and the later evening prayer.
  20:130/q10/p6 Additional voluntary night prayer. — reasons: Razi's second prayer reading treats the night watches as voluntary worship besides five obligatory prayers; Ibn Atiyya includes night voluntary prayer and pre-dawn rakas.
20:130/q11 Why are the night hours singled out? [وَمِنْ ءَانَآئِ ٱلَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ · interpretation]
  20:130/q11/p1 Night worship brings greater focus, seclusion and merit because rest is tempting and effort is greater. — reasons: Kashshaf and Razi invoke 73:6 and 39:9; Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Bursevi repeat the quiet, collected-heart and difficulty grounds. Ibn Ashur says the hours are foregrounded because neglect through rest is likely; Alusi says special importance warrants a renewed command.
20:130/q12 How is min ānāʾ al-layl fasabbiḥ parsed? [وَمِنْ ءَانَآئِ ٱلَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the fronted phrase is governed directly by the following imperative or by an implied verb, and how fa functions.)
  20:130/q12/p1 The fronted partitive or starting-time phrase attaches to the second fasabbiḥ, with fa marking emphasis or necessary sequence. — reasons: Samin attaches the phrase to the second imperative; Ibn Ashur calls min a starting point and fa a response-like emphasis, comparing 17:79 and the hadith about parents; Tabatabai calls min partitive and compares the fronting in 2:40. Alusi reports direct government and explanatory or additional fa, and al-Khafaji says no added fa need be posited.
  20:130/q12/p2 The night-time phrase is governed by an omitted command to rise, after which fasabbiḥ is coordinated. — reasons: Alusi reports this parsing and calls it strained.
  20:130/q12/p3 The phrase can be parsed through coordination with an earlier fronted command, or fa can be explanatory. — reasons: Alusi lists coordination with wa-iyyaya farhabun and alternative explanations of fa.
20:130/q13 Which worship occurs at the day's edges? [وَأَطْرَافَ ٱلنَّهَارِ · interpretation] (turns on: Where the day's ends are placed, whether noon can count as an edge, and whether the command fixes prayer times or covers broad intervals.)
  20:130/q13/p1 The noon or Dhuhr prayer at the boundary of the day's two halves. — reasons: Qatada, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others locate noon at the end of one half and start of the next; Wahidi cites 66:4 for plural wording. Alusi and Tabatabai object that noon is not naturally an edge of the whole day.
  20:130/q13/p2 Both noon and sunset prayers, noon at the meeting of the halves and sunset as a further edge. — reasons: Tabari calls sunset a third edge; Qurtubi and Study Quran repeat the shared-noon-boundary account; Alusi reports a three-edge version; Ibn Ashur allows solar-arc endpoints.
  20:130/q13/p3 Dawn and sunset prayers, repeating periods already named for emphasis. — reasons: Ibn Zayd, Kashshaf, Nasafi and Ibn Jawzi map the two edges this way; Kashshaf compares the specially repeated middle prayer of 2:238. Alusi says this assumes day runs from sunrise to sunset; Ibn Ashur also cites 2:238.
  20:130/q13/p4 Dawn, noon and afternoon prayers or their four day endpoints. — reasons: Farra joins dawn to noon and afternoon, comparing 11:114; Biqai prefers first and last endpoints as dawn and afternoon and middle points as preparation and prayer. Abu Hayyan reports three or four literal-edge counts; Islahi adds chasht and Maghrib in his fuller margin schedule.
  20:130/q13/p5 Daytime voluntary prayers or remembrance across the day's portions. — reasons: Al-Hasan reports voluntary prayer; Razi and Ibn Atiyya add optional prayer; Baydawi and Bursevi extend it across daylight. Alusi rejects a restricted last-hours version as unnatural; Islahi specifically includes chasht.
  20:130/q13/p6 Morning and evening or the day's recurring hours and sides, without fixing a particular prayer. — reasons: Wahidi reports morning-evening and Ibn al-Arabi's hours; Asad relates the extremities to 11:114; Tabatabai prefers broad intervals before sunrise and sunset, whose multiple subparts count as edges relative to noon and avoid repetition.
20:130/q14 Why does the verse use the plural aṭrāf for the day? [أَطْرَافَ ٱلنَّهَارِ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the plural is idiomatic for two, reflects daily recurrence, or counts more actual parts.)
  20:130/q14/p1 Arabic may use a plural for the two ends, including a shared boundary of the day's two halves. — reasons: Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Jawzi and Tabatabai compare the dual hearts in 66:4; Kashshaf invokes the clearer dual in 11:114 and a poetic two-backs example; Razi says the minimum plural can denote two; Samin and Alusi cite poetic parallel. Alusi says two ends are unambiguous for a day and balance plural night hours.
  20:130/q14/p2 The two ends recur every day, so the generic day has a plural set of ends. — reasons: Abu al-Abbas, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Tabatabai report recurrence or day as a genus; Razi cites 11:114.
  20:130/q14/p3 The plural is literal because multiple daytime portions or three or four edges are counted. — reasons: Abu Hayyan reports a three-edge scheme at dawn, noon-afternoon and evening, and a four-edge scheme around sunrise, noon and sunset; Tabari and Alusi count noon's two sides and sunset as a third. Ibn Ashur considers endpoints of the solar arc.
  20:130/q14/p4 Aṭrāf means portions or hours, making the plural straightforward. — reasons: Ibn al-Arabi calls them hours; Samin gives true plural hours; Abu Hayyan reports this, and Alusi cites lexica for taraf as a portion or group. Tabatabai locates several subparts in the broad early and late intervals.
20:130/q15 How is wa-aṭrāfa al-nahār read and syntactically connected? [وَأَطْرَافَ ٱلنَّهَارِ · readings] (turns on: The transmitted case ending and whether the coordination follows an earlier accusative time phrase or the genitive night phrase.)
  20:130/q15/p1 The common accusative coordinates with before sunrise or with the syntactic position of the night-hours phrase. — reasons: Farra, Tabari and Ibn Ashur attach it to the earlier temporal phrase; Kashshaf reports coordination with night hours; Samin and Alusi allow either; Tabatabai supplies an omitted time preposition and calls it comitative.
  20:130/q15/p2 Al-Hasan and Isa ibn Umar read it genitive, coordinated with ānāʾ al-layl. — reasons: Farra considers genitive possible but says it is unreported in his recitation account; Abu Hayyan and Samin name the two readers.
20:130/q16 What is promised by laʿallaka tarḍā? [لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether satisfaction is reward, intercession, broad success, inward acceptance of decree, or divine approval; also whether laʿalla marks hope or assured favor.)
  20:130/q16/p1 The Prophet will be satisfied by divine reward in the Hereafter. — reasons: Yahya transmits al-Hasan's assurance; Ibn Abbas in Wahidi calls it a guaranteed reward and return; Ibn Zayd says additional reward; Abu Hayyan says hope describes reward not yet seen, though another view treats divine hope as certain. Muqatil, Baghawi, Razi, Qurtubi and Study Quran connect satisfaction with recompense for worship; Jishumi says deeds deserve reward.
  20:130/q16/p2 He will be content through intercession for his community or exalted rank. — reasons: Mawardi, Baghawi, Razi, Bursevi and Tabatabai connect intercession to 93:5; Razi also cites 17:79 for elevated favor. Farisi allows God's gift of a high rank.
  20:130/q16/p3 Satisfaction covers God's worldly victory and honor as well as afterlife intercession and Paradise. — reasons: Tabrisi and Tabatabai report the full range of promises; Biqai and Islahi include triumph, fulfillment of hope and success in both lives, comparing 93:5.
  20:130/q16/p4 Persistent glorification leads to inner contentment with God's decree or with whatever He gives. — reasons: Tabatabai prefers this contextual sense and says familiarity with God's acts quiets distraction; Study Quran reports general contentment with worldly gifts; Kur'an Yolu calls its result peace. Qashani describes purification and refinement.
  20:130/q16/p5 God will be pleased with the Prophet or make him pleased through obedient worship or a gift. — reasons: Tabari and Farisi relate the passive to obedience, God-given contentment and 19:55; Baghawi relates divine pleasure to Mary's account; Abu Ubayd prefers the passive because it bears both divine approval and a grant of contentment. Qiraat-ER emphasizes satisfaction as granted.
  20:130/q16/p6 Laʿalla keeps the worshipper hopeful of God's favor without feeling secure, and makes the promised outcome a gracious possibility. — reasons: Biqai stresses hope rather than security; Alusi says the promise does not oblige God to reward, while Abu Hayyan reports the competing view that divine hope necessarily comes true.
20:130/q17 Which command does laʿallaka tarḍā qualify? [لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the final purpose attaches only to worship or to the combined patience-and-worship command.)
  20:130/q17/p1 It qualifies glorification or worship at the named times. — reasons: Bursevi explicitly attaches it to tasbih; Alusi reports this construction as a pleasing reward; Kashshaf takes remembrance at those times as the route to contentment.
  20:130/q17/p2 It qualifies both patience and prayer, with satisfaction through victory and the spread of the mission. — reasons: Alusi reports this wider attachment.
20:130/q18 How is the final verb tarḍā read? [تَرْضَىٰ · readings] (turns on: The vowel of initial tāʾ and the resulting active or passive relation between the Prophet and divine satisfaction.)
  20:130/q18/p1 With fatḥa on tāʾ: that you may be pleased. — reasons: Tabari calls this the majority Medinan and Iraqi reading; Farisi, Ibn Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya list readers and connect it to 93:5. Tabari regards both readings as widespread and equivalent in result; Farra likewise says giving satisfaction and rec
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<20:130 update 1, part 2 of 0..4>>
eiving it converge.
  20:130/q18/p2 With ḍamma on tāʾ: that God may make you pleased, or that you be pleasing to Him. — reasons: Attribution includes al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from Asim across Farisi, Ibn Jawzi, Samin and Nashr; Tabari also names Asim and al-Sulami, and Abu Hayyan and Alusi list further readers. Farisi and Wahidi connect the construction with 19:55; Abu Ubayd prefers its double sense. Qiraat-ER stresses divine grant or approval. Farra reports Abu Abd al-Rahman from Asim; Durr reports raised tāʾ.
20:130/q19 What do reports say about guarding the two prayers before sunrise and sunset? [قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ ٱلشَّمْسِ وَقَبْلَ غُرُوبِهَا · reports] (turns on: These are distinct reports about the same two prayer times, with different promised merits or wording.)
  20:130/q19/p1 The Prophet likened believers' vision of God to seeing the full moon, then urged guarding the two prayers and cited this verse. — reasons: Jarir transmits the report across Yahya, Tabari, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Durr and Bursevi; Ibn Kathir calls it authentic and Biqai says both Sahih collections transmit it.
  20:130/q19/p2 Whoever performs the prayers before sunrise and sunset will not enter the Fire. — reasons: Ibn Kathir cites Muslim through Umara ibn Ruwayba; Durr repeats the report.
  20:130/q19/p3 The Prophet called them the two asr prayers and explained them as prayers before sunrise and sunset. — reasons: Durr and Alusi transmit the instruction to Fadala ibn Wahb.
20:130/q20 What further reports describe divine vision and reward? [لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ · reports] (turns on: The reports describe different events or degrees of heavenly reward.)
  20:130/q20/p1 The highest-ranking person in Paradise sees God twice daily, unlike the lowest rank's thousand-year kingdom. — reasons: Ibn Kathir transmits a report from Ibn Umar.
  20:130/q20/p2 God asks the people of Paradise if they are content, then grants His abiding pleasure. — reasons: Ibn Kathir calls the report authentic.
  20:130/q20/p3 The lifting of the veil and vision of God surpass all prior gifts to Paradise's people. — reasons: Ibn Kathir reports the people recall whitened faces, heavy scales, rescue from Fire and admission to Paradise, then receive the increase of vision.
20:130/q21 What reports or rulings concern prayer practice beyond the fixed times? [وَسَبِّحْ فَسَبِّحْ · law] (turns on: Different reported legal allowances and merits concerning prayer practice.)
  20:130/q21/p1 Prayers may be combined during travel or rain, and advancing them is preferable. — reasons: Jishumi transmits al-Shafi'i's view.
  20:130/q21/p2 Prayers may be combined for occupation and a valid excuse. — reasons: Jishumi transmits al-Hadi's allowance.
  20:130/q21/p3 Combining is allowed generally, while Abu Hanifa distinguishes which prayers may be advanced. — reasons: Jishumi reports these further legal approaches without details of Abu Hanifa's distinctions.
  20:130/q21/p4 Isha and Fajr are hardest on hypocrites, though their reward would bring attendance even by crawling. — reasons: Bursevi transmits the hadith.
  20:130/q21/p5 Keeping the five prayers in congregation brings broad benefits; neglect brings losses. — reasons: Bursevi relays a report without enumerating all its benefits or losses in the note.
  20:130/q21/p6 The community receives mercy and calamities are averted through sincerity, prayer, supplication and weak members. — reasons: Bursevi transmits this hadith and a report that Daniel ascribed rescue from Noah's flood, Ad's wind and Thamud's blast to prayer like this community's.
20:130/q22 How many prescribed prayers does this verse encompass, and when? [وَسَبِّحْ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ ٱلشَّمْسِ وَقَبْلَ غُرُوبِهَا وَمِنْ ءَانَآئِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَأَطْرَافَ ٱلنَّهَارِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the verse is a fixed prayer timetable, includes extra devotions, or uses tasbih more generally; chronology of five prayers is also disputed.)
  20:130/q22/p1 It encompasses all five daily prayers. — reasons: Qatada's common mapping is Fajr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and Dhuhr; Ibn Abbas and Razi assign Dhuhr with Asr before sunset and repeat dawn or sunset at the edges. Razi prefers the five-prayer interpretation among prayer readings; Ibn Ashur relies on mass-transmitted practice. Islahi says the verse rebuts claims that prayer times are absent from the Qur'an, while the Prophet defines each prayer's extent.
  20:130/q22/p2 It names four fixed prayers and omits noon. — reasons: Razi reports the four-prayer interpretation; Tabatabai compares the four-prayer pattern of 11:114 and argues both suras predate the institution of five after the Ascension, citing 17:78.
  20:130/q22/p3 It includes five obligatory prayers and also additional voluntary worship in night and day. — reasons: Razi reports this second prayer reading; Ibn Atiyya and Biqai allow voluntary rites. Islahi specifies tahajjud and ishraq and says extra worship should be maintained in collective or individual hardship.
  20:130/q22/p4 It primarily urges continuous glorification rather than legislating a count of obligatory prayers. — reasons: Tabatabai says the lexicon does not require prescribed prayer; Kur'an Yolu argues five were not yet obligatory in the sura's period and takes thought, word and deed as means of peace.
20:130/q23 What was the historical sequence of obligatory prayer? [وَسَبِّحْ · sciences] (turns on: How the verse's date relates to the development of the five obligatory prayers.)
  20:130/q23/p1 Prayer began as two cycles at dawn and evening; after the Ascension five two-cycle prayers except sunset were imposed, then completed after migration. — reasons: Muqatil reports the sequence.
  20:130/q23/p2 This command predates the obligation of five prayers. — reasons: Durr transmits al-Suddi; Tabatabai dates Ta-Ha and Hud before the post-Ascension al-Isra and suggests four daily prayers then, with five later at 17:78. Kur'an Yolu also uses the earlier date against a five-prayer reading.
20:130/q24 How does this verse connect to its immediate context and other verses? [* · links] (turns on: The sources connect different clauses to prior delay, prayer parallels and later promises.)
  20:130/q24/p1 The fixed but delayed judgment in 20:129 grounds patience in 20:130, followed by worship rather than preoccupation with worldly comfort. — reasons: Tabari and Ibn Ashur explain the prior decree and term; Qashani invokes 8:33 and the Prophet's mercy to explain why the community is spared; Bursevi and Alusi call delay respite. Ibn Ashur and Islahi connect patience and prayer to the warning against coveting comforts and to the God-fearing outcome; Kur'an Yolu reads the sura's end as encouragement under pressure.
  20:130/q24/p2 The command recalls seeking help through patience and prayer in 2:45 and 2:153. — reasons: Razi and Alusi explicitly compare those verses; Tabatabai compares them when explaining contentment with decree.
  20:130/q24/p3 The day-end expressions and repeated prayers are clarified by 11:114, 2:238 and related prayer-time verses. — reasons: Farra, Kashshaf, Razi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai and Asad invoke Hud 11:114 or the middle prayer in 2:238; Bursevi notes parallel discussions at Hud and Qaf.
  20:130/q24/p4 The promised contentment recalls 93:5, with some readings also compared with 19:55 or the high station of 17:79. — reasons: Farisi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Razi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Islahi invoke these promises and prophetic descriptions in arguing over reward, intercession and passive reading.
20:130/q25 Was verse 20:130 revealed in Mecca or Medina? [* · sciences] (turns on: Reports of exceptions to the sura's Meccan classification versus the local style and context.)
  20:130/q25/p1 It belongs with the generally Meccan sura. — reasons: Ibn Ashur reports the majority classify all of Ta-Ha as Meccan; Kur'an Yolu doubts the Medinan reports because the style is Meccan; Study Quran says context supports Mecca.
  20:130/q25/p2 Verses 20:130–131 are Medinan exceptions to the Meccan sura. — reasons: Ibn Ashur reports al-Sakhawi's exception for 20:130 and possible 20:131; Study Quran notes this classification.
